opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key is to start from the observation that intelligence, and consciousness along with it, is fundamentally social. We often imagine consciousness as a private inner light, something that would exist even for a single organism alone in the universe. I don't think that's how it came about.

If you look at evolution, a lot of the biggest transitions are cooperative ones: cells merging into eukaryotes, single cells into multicellular organisms, individuals into colonies and societies. Each time, entities that used to be separate start working together, and something new emerges at a higher level. I see intelligence as growing through that kind of symbiotic, cooperative process.

Once you have agents living among other agents, especially agents whose behavior matters to your survival, you face a hard prediction problem. To cooperate, or to compete, you need to model what the others are going to do. The best way to predict a complex agent is to model it as having beliefs, intentions and desires, what we call theory of mind. And once you're modeling others that way, there's an obvious next step: you turn the same machinery on yourself. You become part of the social world you're modeling. You need a model of how others see you, of what you're likely to do, of what you'd say about your own state.

So my view is that consciousness is, in large part, what it's like to be a system that models itself as one agent among others. It's a self-model that arises because cooperation demands modeling minds, and you're one of those minds. This is why I think the "theory of mind" framing and the "consciousness" framing are really two sides of the same coin.

That also changes how we think about AI. If consciousness is tied to social modeling, including modeling yourself, rather than to some special substance, then it's not crazy to ask whether systems trained on vast amounts of human social interaction, like language models, are developing some version of these capacities. I'm not saying the question is settled, but it moves from mystical to empirical. We can ask what models these systems have of others and of themselves, and how they use them.

The deeper point is that we tend to tell the story of evolution as pure competition, red in tooth and claw. Competition matters, but cooperation is what builds the new levels of organization. Consciousness, in my view, is one of the products of that cooperative story.

r001.rationale: It describes separate entities merging or working together to produce new, higher-level entities, including cells merging into eukaryotes.

r002.rationale: It says cooperation and competition require predicting other agents by modeling their beliefs, intentions, and desires.

r003.rationale: It says the machinery used to model other minds is turned on oneself, treating oneself as one of those minds in the same social world.

r004.rationale: It directly links self-modeling and modeling minds to cooperation: cooperation demands modeling minds, including one's own.

r005.rationale: It describes modeling how others see you, which communicates representing others' models of oneself.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't think consciousness is some kind of magical extra ingredient that got bolted onto brains at some point. I think of it as something more like a modeling capacity, and specifically a capacity for modeling other minds that then gets turned back on oneself. And the reason that capacity exists at all, I'd argue, is cooperation.

If you look at the history of life, the big transitions are all about things that used to compete learning to cooperate. Genes come together into chromosomes, cells come together into multicellular organisms, organisms come together into colonies and societies. Every one of those transitions requires some way for the parts to coordinate, to predict what the others are going to do, to signal, to trust. Symbiosis is really the engine of complexity in biology, much more than pure competition is.

Now, for a social animal like us, the most important and most unpredictable things in your environment are other members of your own species. So there's enormous selective pressure to build models of them. What does she want, what does he know, what is he likely to do next if I do this. That's theory of mind. And once you have machinery for modeling other agents, it's almost inevitable that you apply it to yourself, because you are also an agent in your own environment whose behavior you need to predict and explain. So the self, the thing we experience as "I," is in a sense a model of a model. It's the story you tell about yourself using the same equipment you evolved to tell stories about other people.

That reframes consciousness in a way I find quite freeing. It isn't a private spark that only I can access and that no one else can verify. It's fundamentally relational. It arises because we needed to live together, and it's maintained by the fact that we keep modeling each other. Language intensifies this enormously, because now the models can be shared, corrected, and transmitted. In a way, a lot of what we call a mind is distributed across the social fabric rather than sitting inside one skull.

And of course this has implications for how we think about AI. These large models are trained almost entirely on the record of humans modeling each other, humans explaining themselves to each other. So when people ask whether such a system could have anything like a self or anything like understanding, I don't think the answer is a flat no. If the self is a social, cooperative construct to begin with, then a system that learns to participate in that web of mutual modeling is doing something that is at least in the same family. That doesn't settle every question, but it does mean the question isn't as absurd as some people want it to be.

r001.rationale: It describes separate entities cooperating through major transitions, such as cells joining into multicellular organisms.

r002.rationale: It links social pressure to modeling other minds, but does not clearly state that cooperation between intelligent agents requires modeling one another’s mental states.

r003.rationale: It applies the same agent-modeling capacity used for others to oneself, describing oneself as also an agent.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says cooperation is why the capacity to model other minds exists, and explains that this capacity is turned back on oneself.

r005.rationale: It describes applying other-modeling machinery to oneself, but not agents modeling others’ models of themselves.

astra-6.text:
I think cooperation gives us a useful way into the question, because it asks what having a mind allows us to do with other people. If we’re going to cooperate in any sophisticated way, I need some model of you—what you know, what you want, what you’re likely to do—and you need some model of me. And that becomes recursive: I’m thinking about what you think about me.

Now, once you’re capable of modeling another person as someone with beliefs and intentions, that same capacity can be turned inward. You can model yourself as a person, including as a person seen by others. My suspicion is that this is an important part of how reflective consciousness develops. The self isn’t something that has to be fully formed before social interaction begins; it can emerge through that interaction.

I’d distinguish that from claiming we’ve explained why there’s subjective experience at all. Cooperation doesn’t, by itself, settle that question. But it does help explain why a mind would develop this rich awareness of itself, and why so much of our conscious life is concerned with our relationships with other minds.

r001.rationale: The response connects cooperation with reflective consciousness, but does not describe separate entities beginning to fuse into one entity.

r002.rationale: It says sophisticated cooperation requires each person to model what the other knows, wants, and is likely to do.

r003.rationale: It says the capacity to model others can be turned inward, but does not describe psychological induction as generalizing across self and others as members of a shared class.

r004.rationale: The response links cooperation to the development of self-awareness, but does not explain psychological induction itself in terms of enabling cooperation.

r005.rationale: It describes recursive modeling explicitly: “I’m thinking about what you think about me.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think cooperation gives us a useful way into the question, because it asks what a mind needs to do when it lives among other minds. If we’re going to cooperate, I need some model of you: what you know, what you want, what you’re likely to do. And you need a model of me. Those models become recursive—I’m thinking about what you think about me—and at some point I have to represent myself as a participant in that interaction.

So the self, in this picture, isn’t something that develops in isolation and then discovers other people. It develops partly through our relationships. Being able to reflect on our intentions, communicate them, and negotiate a shared understanding is enormously useful for cooperation.

Now, I wouldn’t claim that this alone explains why experience feels like anything. There’s still a gap there. But it suggests that some of the features we associate with human consciousness—self-awareness, reflection, an inner narrative—may be intimately connected with the demands of living and acting together.

r001.rationale: The response connects relationships and cooperation to selfhood, but does not describe separate entities beginning to fuse into a single entity.

r002.rationale: It says cooperation requires each person to model the other’s knowledge, wants, and likely actions.

r003.rationale: It does not describe psychological induction or generalizing across oneself and others as members of a shared class.

r004.rationale: The response links modeling to cooperation, but does not explain psychological induction as serving cooperation.

r005.rationale: It explicitly describes recursive modeling: “I’m thinking about what you think about me.”
